name: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12
lead: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12, sold as Biopeptide EL, is a synthetic fatty-acid-linked peptide derived from a repeating elastin sequence and used in anti-aging creams. People apply products containing it aiming for firmer, more elastic-looking skin and a smoother appearance of fine lines.

It belongs to the family of cosmetic signal peptides, which includes palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl), a five-amino-acid peptide attached to a 16-carbon fatty chain that the manufacturer Sederma launched in 2000.[3] The fatty chain is described as helping such molecules enter skin lipids.[3]

A 2025 laboratory study using label-free imaging techniques tracked the peptide in full-thickness human skin, found it permeated the stratum corneum and epidermis while forming a gel, and reported that it strengthened and repaired the skin barrier after lipid removal in tests.[1] No clinical trial results were found.

paras: The peptide is promoted in anti-aging products for firmness and elasticity. Researchers describe cosmetic self-assembling peptides of this kind as interacting with skin structures, though their short-term impact on composition and mechanics had been unclear before the 2025 study.[1]

The wider category of palmitoyl matrikine peptides is described as messenger peptides said to activate genes involved in extracellular matrix renewal, an explanation Wikipedia flags as needing citation for Matrixyl.[3]

In the 2025 study, orbital trapping secondary ion mass spectrometry distinguished the peptide's sol and gel forms and tracked its self-assembly and penetration, and stimulated Raman scattering and mechanical testing showed barrier strengthening after delipidation, with co-assembly with native skin molecules shown in vitro and in ex vivo histology.[1] The authors describe the work as a methodological benchmark for measuring cosmetic peptide effects on skin mechanics.[1]
A T Nation member asking about peptides to improve healing times, scarring and results listed TB-500, GHK, Biopeptide EL and Matrixyl together as options.[4]

No studies found in human clinical trials. A 2025 ex vivo study monitored the peptide in human skin layers with non-invasive techniques and assessed its mechanical interaction with skin components.[1]

A 2026 paper proposes a bioinformatic framework for safety evaluation of cosmetic peptides as the industry shifts away from animal testing; it tested palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 along with other cosmetic peptides, and the framework correctly flagged toxin peptides such as amanitin and conotoxin in the same test set.[2] No ingredient-specific adverse-effect data were found.

card.summary: An elastin-fragment cosmetic peptide (Biopeptide EL) with lab-level evidence and no clinical trials found.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is a lab-made peptide based on an elastin sequence, added to anti-ageing creams for elasticity.

Only early laboratory research exists; no clinical trial was found.
quick.mechanism: It is described as a self-assembling peptide that interacts with skin components and may alter skin mechanics, based on a 2025 imaging study.
quick.risks: No ingredient-specific harms were found; safety frameworks for cosmetic peptides are still evolving.

angle.text: People use creams with this peptide hoping for firmer-looking skin and softened fine lines. The 2025 ex vivo study supports penetration and barrier-strengthening in skin samples.
